title: SAGE: A Unified Framework for Generalizable Object State Recognition with S

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'We enforce that at least half of the selected concepts are shared. Specifically, to select k concepts, we first select the top-ranked shared concepts until floor(k/2) are selected...' and then says 'In practice, we select the top 5 concepts for each object state and ensure that at least 3 of them are shared.' For k=5, floor(k/2)=2, not 3, and 2/5=40% is less than half, contradicting the stated 'at least half' requirement. The formula and the stated practical implementation are mathematically inconsistent with each other and with the stated design goal.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 5, 'ChangeIt % Pre@1 (△) Novel Obj & Act' column
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reconstructing the implied full-model (SAGE) baseline from each ablation row's reported value plus delta should yield a single consistent number, since all rows are deltas relative to the same complete model. However: 'W/o Visual Descriptions' 48.4 (-7.0) implies baseline 55.4; 'W/o Joint Training' 47.9 (-4.1) implies baseline 52.0; 'W/o Dynamic State Locating' 48.8 (-3.2) implies baseline 52.0. The baseline implied by the Visual Descriptions row (55.4) is inconsistent with the baseline implied by the other two rows (52.0) in the same column, an internal arithmetic contradiction.

The ablation deltas in Table 5 consistently imply a full-model 'Seen' performance of 61.4% for ChangeIt and 54.8% for HowToChange (e.g., 49.8+11.6=61.4; 56.8+4.6=61.4; 46.4+8.4=54.8; 50.7+4.1=54.8), and a 'Novel Obj' baseline of 57.1% (ChangeIt) and 49.7% (HowToChange). However, Table 1 reports the full unprivileged SAGE model's ChangeIt State Pre@1 as 0.51 and Trans. Pre@1 as 0.81, and HowToChange Pre@1 as 0.52; Table 2a reports ChangeIt Novel Obj State Pre@1 as 0.49. None of these match the values implied by Table 5's ablation deltas, indicating the two tables describe different (and inconsistent) 'full model' performance numbers.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1 (Introduction): 'SAGE outperforms the prior state-of-the-art (Xue et al., 2024) across all benchmarks'; Section 5 (Conclusion): 'Our model outperforms all baselines on two widely used object state transformation benchmarks'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Appendix Table A9 reports several non-significant or exactly tied comparisons between SAGE and VidOSC (e.g., State Pre@1 p=2.7e-01 (✗), Trans. Pre@1 seen p=1.0e+00 (✗), F1 seen p=1.0e+00 (✗), Precision seen p=3.5e-01 (✗)), directly contradicting the blanket claim that SAGE 'outperforms... across all benchmarks.' The tied p-values correspond to identical reported values in Table 7 (e.g., Trans. predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Introduction: '14.6% relative precision gain on novel state recognition'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The 14.6% figure can only be reproduced from Table 7 (ChangeIt State Pre@1, 'novel' column: (0.55-0.48)/0.48=14.6%), which uses a different backbone (VideoCLIP, not the paper's main CLIP ViT-L-14 backbone) and evaluates only novel objects (not novel actions), per Table 7's own open-world protocol. Yet the Introduction frames this gain as applying to 'objects and actions unseen during training,' which corresponds to the harder Novel-Obj-and-Act setting in Table 2b under the main CLIP backbone, where the actual relative gain over VidOSC* is far larger (e.g., State Pre@1: (0.45-0.27)/0.27=66.7%). This selectively quotes a smaller, non-representative number while describing it as representative of the harder generalization setting.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2 (Related Work): '(Menon and Vondrick, 2022; Pratt et al., 2023; Zang et al., 2025)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The in-text citation lists 'Menon and Vondrick, 2022,' but the reference list entry reads 'Sachit Menon and Carl Vondrick. 2023. Visual classification via description from large language models. In The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations.' The cited year (2022) does not match the reference list year (2023).

Table 4's 'before refinement' (5 concepts) row (Known F1=0.37, Pre=0.42, Pre@1=0.55) matches Table 1's SAGE (action-privileged, object-unprivileged) row exactly, while its Novel values (F1=0.31, Pre=0.35, Pre@1=0.45) do not match Table 2a's SAGE Novel-Object row (F1=0.34, Pre=0.39, Pre@1=0.50). Conversely, Table 4's 'after refinement' row Novel values (0.33, 0.39, 0.50) match Table 2a almost exactly, but its Known values (0.38, 0.42, 0.58) do not match Table 1 (0.37, 0.42, 0.55). This suggests Table 1 and Table 2 report results from inconsistent versions (before vs. after refinement) of the same nominally 'final' SAGE model, which is methodologically contradictory since refinement is presented as the proposed final design.

The caption states 'variance is observed across multiple runs with standard deviations up to 3%, indicating some overlap in performance ranges,' but no standard deviations, error bars, or multiple-run results are reported anywhere in the table or the surrounding text, making this a statistical claim unsupported by any presented data.

The paper states 'we use OpenAI GPT-4o-mini-2024-07-18 as the LLM... We also experiment with an open-weight model, Qwen3-32B, and find the performance differences are negligible compared to GPT-4o.' The comparison model actually used throughout is GPT-4o-mini, not the full GPT-4o, so describing the comparison as being against 'GPT-4o' misattributes/misstates the model actually used in the main experiments.
